scams.name: Fort Lauderdale (FLL) Airport & Port Everglades Cruise Taxi Overcharge
scams.description:
A common piece of local advice runs simply: do not use taxis outside the Fort Lauderdale airport. The pattern is consistent. Drivers at FLL baggage claim and the Port Everglades cruise terminals solicit cruise passengers with offers of a "flat $40–$60" to the port or to downtown hotels, when legitimate rideshare runs $15–$28 and a licensed metered taxi runs $18–$32. As of 2025, the FLL taxi-pricing picture favors the meter for short hops: a YellowCab metered fare runs cheaper than Uber during surge pricing for the run to Port Everglades (3 miles, roughly $18 by taxi versus $25 or more for a surge Uber). A common "limo" tout charges $100 or more for a standard 10-minute trip.

The scam has several variants: (1) a driver insisting the meter is "broken"; (2) a "cruise ship surcharge" added on top of the metered rate; (3) a "limo" or "black car" tout quoting $100 or more for a standard trip; and (4) a shared-ride operator charging $50 or more per person for a trip that Uber Pool does for $12.

For older travelers, especially cruise passengers arriving at or departing from FLL or Port Everglades, the clean playbook is this: (1) take an Uber or Lyft at the designated rideshare pickup zones — FLL Terminal 1/2/3 curb level 2, or the Port Everglades cruise terminal designated rideshare zone ($15–$28 with a fare screenshot); (2) use a licensed YellowCab metered taxi at the official taxi queue, which runs $18–$32 from FLL to Port Everglades and $25–$40 from FLL to downtown Fort Lauderdale beach; (3) during peak Uber surge pricing, such as Saturday cruise-turnaround days, compare the taxi-stand rate, which is often cheaper; (4) refuse drivers soliciting at baggage claim with a "flat rate" offer, and walk to the official taxi queue instead; (5) for a shared shuttle, pre-book GO Airport Shuttle at goairportshuttle.com ($22 per person to the cruise port); and (6) Broward County Transit route 1 connects FLL to Port Everglades for $2 — schedule-limited, but scam-proof.
scams.avoidance: Take an Uber or Lyft at the designated rideshare zones, with a fare screenshot ($15–$28). Use a licensed YellowCab metered taxi ($18–$32 from FLL to the port). Pre-book GO Airport Shuttle at goairportshuttle.com ($22 per person). Broward County Transit route 1 is $2 (schedule-limited). Compare the Uber surge rate against the taxi stand during Saturday turnaround peaks.
scams.location: FLL baggage claim taxi solicitors, Port Everglades cruise terminal taxi queue, Terminal 1/2/3 'limo' touts, airport-adjacent 'express' shuttle operators
scams.tldr: Drivers at FLL baggage claim and Port Everglades solicit cruise passengers with "flat $40–$60" fares when rideshare runs $15–$28 and metered taxi runs $18–$32. Variants include a "broken" meter, a "cruise ship surcharge," $100-plus "limo" touts, and shared-ride operators charging $50-plus per person.

scams.name: FLL Airport 'Skysquad' / 'VIP Assistance' & Baggage Bait-Switch Scam
scams.description:
Travelers report a specific pattern at FLL: "Skysquad" and similar "VIP airport assistance" services offered at Spirit Airlines check-in are sold as "airport concierge" at $45–$150 per person. They are advertised as "TSA PreCheck fast-track + baggage assistance + gate escort," but in practice provide nothing beyond pushing a luggage cart.

More serious variants exist: (1) reports of FLL baggage-handler theft from checked luggage, including a 2024 felony charge against an airport employee; and (2) a cross-airport bag-swap pattern in which a stranger "accidentally" takes your bag at baggage claim, then returns it with valuables missing.

For older travelers at FLL, the defensive playbook is this: (1) refuse "Skysquad," "VIP assistance," and "airport concierge" solicitations at check-in — if you need mobility assistance, request free wheelchair or motorized cart service through your airline 48 hours before departure, at no charge; (2) TSA PreCheck fast-track costs $85 for a 5-year membership through tsa.gov, and no "day pass" exists; (3) lock checked luggage with TSA-approved locks, and carry valuables, electronics, medications, and documents in your carry-on; (4) at baggage claim, verify that the bag tag matches your claim receipt before walking away, and never grab "a similar bag"; (5) if your checked bag arrives with theft damage, report it at the airline's baggage office within 4 hours and file an FAA report immediately; and (6) photograph high-value items before check-in as evidence for any theft claim.
scams.avoidance: Refuse "Skysquad" and "VIP assistance" solicitations. Request free airline wheelchair or mobility cart service 48 hours before your flight. Get TSA PreCheck only through tsa.gov ($85 for 5 years) — no day passes exist. Lock checked bags with TSA-approved locks and keep valuables in your carry-on. Verify that the bag tag matches your claim receipt before leaving baggage claim.
scams.location: FLL Terminal 1 Spirit Airlines check-in, Terminal 3/4 gate areas, baggage claim exit corridors, Customs arrivals hallway
scams.tldr: At Spirit check-in, "Skysquad" and "VIP assistance" services sell "airport concierge" at $45–$150 per person but deliver nothing beyond pushing a luggage cart. More serious variants include baggage-handler theft (a 2024 felony charge against an airport employee) and a bag-swap pattern at baggage claim.

scams.name: ACA Group Timeshare Fort Lauderdale & 'Won a Vacation' Presentation Hustle
scams.description:
Fort Lauderdale has a well-documented timeshare operation (ACA Group) and a recurring "won a vacation" pattern: (1) a promoter calls or mails to claim, "You won a free Fort Lauderdale beach vacation!"; (2) the "vacation" requires attending a 90-minute "presentation" upon arrival; (3) the presentation actually runs 3 to 6 hours, with aggressive pressure to buy $10,000–$50,000 "vacation ownership" or "travel club" packages; and (4) the target is older travelers perceived to have disposable retirement funds. Variants operate under the names ACA Group, Westgate Resorts Las Olas, and Diamond Resorts Fort Lauderdale. There is also a related "travel club" variant sold as "10 dream weeks, lifetime valid."

For older travelers in Fort Lauderdale, the defensive posture is this: (1) never respond to a "You won a free vacation" letter, phone call, or email — 100 percent of these are timeshare-presentation hooks; (2) if you have already committed, bring a printed "I will not sign anything today" rule and stick to it; (3) if you signed under pressure, Florida offers a 10-day right of rescission for timeshare contracts, so cancel within 10 days by certified mail — Florida is more generous than most states; (4) for rescission help, contact Florida Attorney General Consumer Protection (myfloridalegal.com), not "exit" companies charging $5,000–$15,000; (5) report ACA Group or similar operations to the Florida AG, the Broward BBB, and the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov; and (6) once you account for the time cost and the pressure, the "cheap vacation" math comes out net negative.
scams.avoidance: Never respond to "You won a free vacation" offers — all are timeshare hooks. If you attend, bring an "I will not sign anything today" rule and stick to it. Use Florida's 10-day right of rescission (the most generous in the US). Report to the Florida AG (myfloridalegal.com), the Broward BBB, and the FTC. Avoid "exit" companies charging $5,000 or more; use the state AG instead.
scams.location: ACA Group office Fort Lauderdale, Las Olas Blvd timeshare kiosks, Fort Lauderdale beach resort lobbies, Galleria Mall promoter booths
scams.tldr: A Fort Lauderdale timeshare operation (ACA Group) and a "won a vacation" pitch lure older travelers with a "free beach vacation" that requires a "90-minute presentation," which actually runs 3 to 6 hours of aggressive pressure to buy $10,000–$50,000 ownership or travel-club packages.

scams.name: Fort Lauderdale Beach Parking Tickets & 'Parking Services' Overcharge
scams.description:
Fort Lauderdale Beach has aggressive parking enforcement, and newer patterns have emerged in 2024 and 2025. The issues are these: (1) metered parking on Fort Lauderdale Beach requires the ParkMobile app, and some blocks allow only a 2-hour maximum for tourists, with residents-only signs posted sparingly; (2) enforcement tows vehicles within 1 hour of expiration, with release fees of $300 or more; (3) some "privately operated" beach parking lots on A1A advertise "$10 all-day" and then add an "overnight fee" or "exit fee" when you leave; (4) legitimate city-operated parking includes the Fort Lauderdale Aquatic Complex Garage ($2 per hour), Las Olas Beach Parking ($3 per hour), and Beach Place Garage ($2.50 per hour); and (5) fake "parking tickets" placed on windshields carry a payment URL that leads to a scam website — the actual city accepts online payment only through ftlauderdale.gov.

For older travelers driving to Fort Lauderdale Beach, the clean playbook is this: (1) park at legitimate city garages — the Aquatic Complex ($2 per hour), Las Olas Beach ($3 per hour), or Beach Place ($2.50 per hour) — and skip street parking entirely; (2) if you use meters, download the ParkMobile app and set expiration reminders; (3) avoid "privately operated" beach lots with handwritten "$10 all-day" signs, since legitimate city lots have digital pay stations; (4) if you get a ticket, pay only through ftlauderdale.gov or in person at the Municipal Code Compliance office, never through a URL on a windshield notice; and (5) tow release fees run $300 or more, so an hour of garage parking at $2–$3 is far cheaper insurance.
scams.avoidance: Park at legitimate city garages: the Aquatic Complex, Las Olas Beach, or Beach Place ($2–$3 per hour). Download ParkMobile for meters and set expiration reminders. Avoid privately operated "all-day" lots with handwritten signs. Pay tickets only at ftlauderdale.gov or the Municipal Code Compliance office. Garage parking is cheaper than a $300-plus tow release fee.
scams.location: Fort Lauderdale beach metered parking, Las Olas Blvd parking garages, A1A beachfront meters, Sunrise Blvd parking enforcement zones
scams.tldr: Fort Lauderdale Beach has aggressive parking enforcement: 2-hour ParkMobile meter limits, tows within 1 hour of expiration ($300-plus release fees), "privately operated" lots advertising "$10 all-day" that add exit fees, and fake windshield tickets with payment URLs leading to scam websites.

scams.name: Fort Lauderdale Beach Hotel 'Resort Fee' & Las Olas STR Surcharge Scam
scams.description:
Fort Lauderdale draws ongoing local complaints about opaque "resort fees" and hotel surcharges. The patterns are these: (1) a "resort fee" of $25–$55 per night added at check-in rather than at booking, covering "WiFi, pool, beach chair" (often used for amenities that are free elsewhere); (2) a "destination fee" of $15–$30, separate from the resort fee; (3) a "parking fee" of $25–$45 per night, even for self-parking; (4) a "WiFi premium" of $10–$15 per day for basic internet; and (5) a "housekeeping gratuity" of $5–$10 per day, automatically added. For short-term rentals: (6) Airbnb "cleaning fees" of $150–$350 for 2-night stays, when $50–$150 would be fair; (7) off-platform "discount beach rental" offers that ask for Zelle or Venmo, which are fraud, following the universal off-platform pattern; and (8) Booking.com listings advertising a "Fort Lauderdale beach view" that are actually 3 blocks inland.

For older travelers booking Fort Lauderdale accommodation, the protective playbook is this: (1) when comparing hotels, add the "resort fee," "destination fee," and "parking" to the headline rate — a $199 room at Pier 66 becomes $275 with typical add-ons; (2) check resortfeechecker.com before booking to see the actual all-in cost; (3) for short-term rentals, book only through the Airbnb, VRBO, or Booking.com platform payment system, never through Zelle, Venmo, or wire transfer; (4) legitimate Fort Lauderdale beachfront hotels include Pier 66, the W Fort Lauderdale, the Ritz-Carlton, the Marriott Harbor Beach, and the Hyatt Centric Las Olas; (5) if a "resort fee" was not disclosed in your booking, dispute it at check-in and with your credit card company; and (6) if a "housekeeping gratuity" is automatically added at a short-term rental or hotel, request its removal and tip in cash directly if you want to tip.
scams.avoidance: Add the resort, destination, and parking fees to the headline rate when comparing. Check resortfeechecker.com for the actual all-in cost. Book short-term rentals only through Airbnb, VRBO, or Booking.com platform payment. Legitimate hotels include Pier 66, the W, the Ritz-Carlton, the Marriott Harbor Beach, and the Hyatt Centric. Dispute undisclosed resort fees at check-in and with your credit card.
scams.location: Fort Lauderdale Beach hotels (A1A strip), Las Olas Blvd boutique hotels, Pier 66 / Hyatt / Marriott resort fees, STR beach rentals
scams.tldr: Fort Lauderdale hotels add opaque charges at check-in: "resort fees" of $25–$55 a night, "destination fees" of $15–$30, parking fees of $25–$45, WiFi premiums, and auto-added housekeeping gratuities. Short-term rentals add inflated cleaning fees and off-platform Zelle/Venmo offers that are fraud.

scams.name: FLL Spirit Airlines 'Carry-On Fee' & Baggage Upsell Scam
scams.description:
Spirit Airlines is FLL's dominant budget carrier, and its ultra-low-cost model, combined with an aggressive fee structure, creates a consistently scam-adjacent experience for unsuspecting travelers. The pattern is this: (1) the fare purchased online does not include a carry-on bag ($38–$65) or a checked bag ($42–$80); (2) gate agents enforce the size-sizer templates strictly, charging a $99 "gate-size violation fee" if a carry-on exceeds the template by any amount; (3) a "seat selection" fee of $7–$199 per seat is the only way to sit with a travel companion; (4) "priority boarding" costs $6–$17; and (5) water and food are charged for on the flight. Spirit's model is legitimate rather than an outright scam, but many older travelers do not realize these fees until checkout.

For older travelers flying Spirit from FLL, the protective playbook is this: (1) budget the total cost realistically — fare plus carry-on ($38–$65) plus seat ($7–$199) plus any checked bag ($42–$80), which often reaches $60–$250 over the headline fare; (2) pay the carry-on and checked-bag fees during online booking, the cheapest tier, since adding them at the airport costs $15–$30 more and at the gate costs $99 or more; (3) measure your carry-on at home, because Spirit's 22-by-18-by-10-inch personal item limit is smaller than most carriers'; (4) if budget matters, compare Southwest (2 checked bags free) or Delta Basic Economy at a similar total cost; (5) for FLL domestic flights, JetBlue and Southwest offer honest pricing that includes a carry-on; and (6) Spirit's "Saver's Club" at $70 per year pays off only if you fly Spirit 4 or more times per year.
scams.avoidance: Budget Spirit's total realistically: fare plus $40–$200 in fees. Pay carry-on and checked-bag fees during online booking (the cheapest tier). Measure your carry-on at home against Spirit's 22-by-18-by-10-inch personal item limit. Compare Southwest or JetBlue for honest total-cost pricing from FLL. The Spirit Saver's Club ($70 per year) only pays off if you fly Spirit 4 or more times per year.
scams.location: FLL Terminal 1 Spirit Airlines check-in counter, Spirit Airlines boarding gates, Ticket-counter baggage fee kiosks
scams.tldr: Spirit's ultra-low-cost fares exclude carry-on ($38–$65) and checked bags ($42–$80), with a $99 gate-size violation fee, $7–$199 seat selection, paid priority boarding, and on-flight charges for water and food. The model is legitimate, but the fees often catch older travelers by surprise at checkout.
